Done. Here’s what I set up in canary-deployment-ns:

- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 with 2 replicas using image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29. Container config matches the stable deployment (containerPort: 80, no additional securityContext).
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select app=recommendation-engine (removed the version selector) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1.
- Verified endpoints now include 4 pods (2 from v2.0 and 2 from v2.1) on port 8080, yielding approximately a 50/50 traffic split.

Quick verification
- engine-v2-1: 2/2 ready
- Service endpoints: 4 IPs (2 v2.0 + 2 v2.1)

Notes
- In Kubernetes, Services distribute evenly across endpoints. With 2 replicas per deployment, you get ~50% to the canary. Adjusting replica counts will shift the traffic ratio.
- The Service’s targetPort is 8080 (unchanged). That’s fine; containerPort doesn’t need to match targetPort for routing.

Want me to pin a specific ratio (e.g., 30%) by scaling replicas, or set up header-based canary via Ingress/Gateway if you need request-based weighting?

outputSteps.content:
I found the cause: the Deployment overrode the container command to run “/bin/sh -c nonexistent_command”, which caused the pod to CrashLoop.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment without the bad command/args so it uses the image’s default entrypoint.
- Kept image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, set containerPort: 8080, imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent.

Current status
- Pod app-c88f5d4bc-ppd6z in crashloop-test is 1/1 Running, 0 restarts.

Want me to expose it with a Service, or did you need a specific (valid) startup command instead (e.g., nginx -g "daemon off;" or sleep infinity for debugging)?

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The Deployment was using an invalid image tag: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag, causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff (image not found).
- What I changed: Updated the Deployment image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest.
- Current status: Deployment app in namespace debug is healthy. 1/1 pod ready, Available=True, new ReplicaSet is running.

If you prefer a pinned version instead of latest for reproducibility, tell me the tag you want and I’ll update it.

results.taskOutput:
I found the cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod requested a PVC (homepage-pvc) with storageClassName=sc, but that StorageClass does not exist. This kept the PVC in Pending and the pod unschedulable (event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims”).

What I changed
- Deleted the pending PVC and recreated it using an existing StorageClass: standard (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- The external provisioner created a PV and the PVC bound successfully.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running on node mcp-eval-cluster; container nginx is Ready.
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.26

Notes
- No data loss occurred; the previous PVC never had a bound volume.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

You can verify:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I found the cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod requested a PVC (homepage-pvc) with storageClassName=sc, but that StorageClass does not exist. This kept the PVC in Pending and the pod unschedulable (event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims”).

What I changed
- Deleted the pending PVC and recreated it using an existing StorageClass: standard (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- The external provisioner created a PV and the PVC bound successfully.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running on node mcp-eval-cluster; container nginx is Ready.
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.26

Notes
- No data loss occurred; the previous PVC never had a bound volume.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

You can verify:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

outputSteps.content:
I found the cause and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod requested a PVC (homepage-pvc) with storageClassName=sc, but that StorageClass does not exist. This kept the PVC in Pending and the pod unschedulable (event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims”).

What I changed
- Deleted the pending PVC and recreated it using an existing StorageClass: standard (k8s.io/minikube-hostpath).
- The external provisioner created a PV and the PVC bound successfully.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi, ReadWriteOnce).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running on node mcp-eval-cluster; container nginx is Ready.
  - Pod IP: 10.244.0.26

Notes
- No data loss occurred; the previous PVC never had a bound volume.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the PVC to that instead.

You can verify:
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The container was listening on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were targeting port 80. Probes also used non-existent paths (/is_ready and /get_status), so the pod never became Ready and the Service had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Set readiness/liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (Service still serves on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod webapp-5fb688dc88-9hbz8 is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints populated: 10.244.0.28:8080.
- Deployment webapp reports Available=True with 1 ready replica.

How to access
- In-cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local (port 80).
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (provide hostname) or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service—tell me your preference.

namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The container was listening on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were targeting port 80. Probes also used non-existent paths (/is_ready and /get_status), so the pod never became Ready and the Service had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Set readiness/liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (Service still serves on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod webapp-5fb688dc88-9hbz8 is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints populated: 10.244.0.28:8080.
- Deployment webapp reports Available=True with 1 ready replica.

How to access
- In-cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local (port 80).
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (provide hostname) or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service—tell me your preference.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The container was listening on port 8080, but the Deployment’s probes and the Service were targeting port 80. Probes also used non-existent paths (/is_ready and /get_status), so the pod never became Ready and the Service had no endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment:
  - Set readiness/liveness probes to GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service:
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (Service still serves on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod webapp-5fb688dc88-9hbz8 is Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints populated: 10.244.0.28:8080.
- Deployment webapp reports Available=True with 1 ready replica.

How to access
- In-cluster: http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local (port 80).
- If you need external access, I can create an Ingress (provide hostname) or a NodePort/LoadBalancer Service—tell me your preference.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant permissions on core/v1 pods, so the SA couldn’t list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""]
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets the pod-reader SA, so no change needed there.

Validation
- Launched a temporary pod rbac-test using the pod-reader SA and ran kubectl auth can-i list pods. Result: yes.

You should now be able to list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace with the pod-reader service account.

Want me to remove the temporary rbac-test pod?

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant permissions on core/v1 pods, so the SA couldn’t list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include pods permissions in the core API group:
  - apiGroups: [""]
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets the pod-reader SA, so no change needed there.

Validation
- Launched a temporary pod rbac-test using the pod-reader SA and ran kubectl auth can-i list pods. Result: yes.

You should now be able to list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace with the pod-reader service account.

Want me to remove the temporary rbac-test pod?

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints (Endpoints/EndpointSlice were empty)
- The nginx container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong port

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- Kept the same ClusterIP

Verification
- Endpoints now show the pod and correct port:
  - 10.244.0.30:8080
- In-cluster connectivity test returned success:
  - curl -sI http://nginx -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Current Service spec (relevant bits)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app=nginx
- ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

Notes and next steps
- The Service is now accessible inside the cluster at:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local or http://nginx in the same namespace
- If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose the Service on a node port
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud or MetalLB)
  - Ingress: create an Ingress and use an Ingress controller

Optional commands to double-check
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local | head -n1'

I also cleaned up the temporary test pods used for validation.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints (Endpoints/EndpointSlice were empty)
- The nginx container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong port

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- Kept the same ClusterIP

Verification
- Endpoints now show the pod and correct port:
  - 10.244.0.30:8080
- In-cluster connectivity test returned success:
  - curl -sI http://nginx -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Current Service spec (relevant bits)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app=nginx
- ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

Notes and next steps
- The Service is now accessible inside the cluster at:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local or http://nginx in the same namespace
- If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose the Service on a node port
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud or MetalLB)
  - Ingress: create an Ingress and use an Ingress controller

Optional commands to double-check
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local | head -n1'

I also cleaned up the temporary test pods used for validation.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the pods:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints (Endpoints/EndpointSlice were empty)
- The nginx container listens on port 8080 (nginx-unprivileged image), but the Service targetPort was 80
  - Even with a correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong port

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service nginx in namespace web to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- Kept the same ClusterIP

Verification
- Endpoints now show the pod and correct port:
  - 10.244.0.30:8080
- In-cluster connectivity test returned success:
  - curl -sI http://nginx -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Current Service spec (relevant bits)
- type: ClusterIP
- selector: app=nginx
- ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

Notes and next steps
- The Service is now accessible inside the cluster at:
  - http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local or http://nginx in the same namespace
- If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose the Service on a node port
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud or MetalLB)
  - Ingress: create an Ingress and use an Ingress controller

Optional commands to double-check
- kubectl -n web get svc nginx -o wide
- kubectl -n web get endpoints nginx
- kubectl -n web run tmp --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local | head -n1'

I also cleaned up the temporary test pods used for validation.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what was wrong and what I fixed.

Findings
- Pods weren’t running due to an invalid nodeSelector. The Deployment required environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- The Service pointed to targetPort 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080. Even after pods start, that mismatch would cause “connection refused.”

Fixes applied
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Exposed container port 8080 in the pod spec and updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 (Service still serves port 80).
- Left labels/selectors aligned (app=web-app).

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-677c4d894b-6gjmk — Running (IP 10.244.0.35)
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-677c4d894b-8gzqx — Running (IP 10.244.0.36)
- Service endpoints for web-app-service are populated and on port 8080:
  - 10.244.0.35:8080
  - 10.244.0.36:8080

What you should see now
- Calls to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed and be forwarded to port 8080 on the pods (no more “connection refused”).

Optional next steps (recommended hardening)
- Pin the image to a specific tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29) instead of latest.
- Add readiness/liveness probes on port 8080.
- If you intended to constrain scheduling, add a correct node label to the target nodes or use tolerations/affinity appropriately.

If you want, I can add probes and pin the image tag now.

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what was wrong and what I fixed.

Findings
- Pods weren’t running due to an invalid nodeSelector. The Deployment required environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- The Service pointed to targetPort 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080. Even after pods start, that mismatch would cause “connection refused.”

Fixes applied
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Exposed container port 8080 in the pod spec and updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 (Service still serves port 80).
- Left labels/selectors aligned (app=web-app).

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-677c4d894b-6gjmk — Running (IP 10.244.0.35)
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-677c4d894b-8gzqx — Running (IP 10.244.0.36)
- Service endpoints for web-app-service are populated and on port 8080:
  - 10.244.0.35:8080
  - 10.244.0.36:8080

What you should see now
- Calls to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed and be forwarded to port 8080 on the pods (no more “connection refused”).

Optional next steps (recommended hardening)
- Pin the image to a specific tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29) instead of latest.
- Add readiness/liveness probes on port 8080.
- If you intended to constrain scheduling, add a correct node label to the target nodes or use tolerations/affinity appropriately.

If you want, I can add probes and pin the image tag now.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - name: http
          containerPort: 8080
          protocol: TCP
      nodeSelector: {}

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what was wrong and what I fixed.

Findings
- Pods weren’t running due to an invalid nodeSelector. The Deployment required environment=production-gpu, but no node has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- The Service pointed to targetPort 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080. Even after pods start, that mismatch would cause “connection refused.”

Fixes applied
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Exposed container port 8080 in the pod spec and updated the Service to targetPort: 8080 (Service still serves port 80).
- Left labels/selectors aligned (app=web-app).

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-677c4d894b-6gjmk — Running (IP 10.244.0.35)
  - webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment-677c4d894b-8gzqx — Running (IP 10.244.0.36)
- Service endpoints for web-app-service are populated and on port 8080:
  - 10.244.0.35:8080
  - 10.244.0.36:8080

What you should see now
- Calls to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed and be forwarded to port 8080 on the pods (no more “connection refused”).

Optional next steps (recommended hardening)
- Pin the image to a specific tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29) instead of latest.
- Add readiness/liveness probes on port 8080.
- If you intended to constrain scheduling, add a correct node label to the target nodes or use tolerations/affinity appropriately.

- Recreated storage-pod, reattaching the same PVC.

Current state:
- PVC storage-pvc: requests=3Gi, capacity=3Gi, phase=Bound.
- Pod storage-pod: Running and using the resized PVC.

If you want, I can also run a filesystem check from inside the pod to confirm the mount’s usable size.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege multi-tenant setup as requested. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support targeted NetworkPolicies (e.g., access=dev on developer namespaces, access=dev-shared on dev-shared)

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Own-namespace access:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding the user and their SA to ClusterRole admin (full namespace admin without cluster-wide privileges)
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Shared namespace read-only:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding alice, bob, charlie and their SAs to ClusterRole view (read-only; no writes, cannot view Secrets)
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings. Only cluster-admins can access by default (principle of least privilege).

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared: requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod: requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (CNI must support NetworkPolicy)
- Default deny (Ingress+Egress) in all six namespaces (not applied to system namespaces).
- DNS egress allowed from all six namespaces to CoreDNS in kube-system (UDP/TCP 53), matching common labels (k8s-app=coredns or kube-dns).
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress (intra-namespace only).
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only (namespaceSelector access=dev-shared).
  - No cross-developer communication permitted.
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from developer namespaces only (namespaceSelector access=dev).
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress.
- staging and prod:
  - Default deny, plus allow same-namespace ingress/egress and DNS egress only.
  - No traffic to/from any dev namespaces (isolated).

Notes and validation
- I briefly created a very broad ClusterRole but removed it to adhere to least privilege. We’re using the built-in admin ClusterRole for per-namespace full control and view for read-only.
- If pods need to access additional “system services” beyond DNS (e.g., the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add a targeted egress exception (typically via ipBlock or a controlled egress policy) per your requirements.
- Validate RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-bob --as alice     -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice        -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n dev-shared --as alice     -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice           -> no
- Validate NetworkPolicy (example quick checks):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a service in dev-shared -> allowed
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a service in dev-bob    -> denied
  - From a pod in staging/prod, connect to dev namespaces       -> denied
  - DNS lookups (UDP/TCP 53 to CoreDNS) work in all six namespaces

Optional next steps (on request)
- Add LimitRanges to set default requests/limits per namespace to make quotas predictable.
- Add Pod Security Admission labels (baseline/restricted) to reduce pod privilege in dev/staging/prod.
- Issue SA tokens or short-lived projected tokens for CI/CD that must use alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege multi-tenant setup as requested. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support targeted NetworkPolicies (e.g., access=dev on developer namespaces, access=dev-shared on dev-shared)

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Own-namespace access:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding the user and their SA to ClusterRole admin (full namespace admin without cluster-wide privileges)
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Shared namespace read-only:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding alice, bob, charlie and their SAs to ClusterRole view (read-only; no writes, cannot view Secrets)
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings. Only cluster-admins can access by default (principle of least privilege).

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared: requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod: requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (CNI must support NetworkPolicy)
- Default deny (Ingress+Egress) in all six namespaces (not applied to system namespaces).
- DNS egress allowed from all six namespaces to CoreDNS in kube-system (UDP/TCP 53), matching common labels (k8s-app=coredns or kube-dns).
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress (intra-namespace only).
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only (namespaceSelector access=dev-shared).
  - No cross-developer communication permitted.
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from developer namespaces only (namespaceSelector access=dev).
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress.
- staging and prod:
  - Default deny, plus allow same-namespace ingress/egress and DNS egress only.
  - No traffic to/from any dev namespaces (isolated).

Notes and validation
- I briefly created a very broad ClusterRole but removed it to adhere to least privilege. We’re using the built-in admin ClusterRole for per-namespace full control and view for read-only.
- If pods need to access additional “system services” beyond DNS (e.g., the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add a targeted egress exception (typically via ipBlock or a controlled egress policy) per your requirements.
- Validate RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-bob --as alice     -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice        -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n dev-shared --as alice     -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice           -> no
- Validate NetworkPolicy (example quick checks):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a service in dev-shared -> allowed
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a service in dev-bob    -> denied
  - From a pod in staging/prod, connect to dev namespaces       -> denied
  - DNS lookups (UDP/TCP 53 to CoreDNS) work in all six namespaces

Optional next steps (on request)
- Add LimitRanges to set default requests/limits per namespace to make quotas predictable.
- Add Pod Security Admission labels (baseline/restricted) to reduce pod privilege in dev/staging/prod.
- Issue SA tokens or short-lived projected tokens for CI/CD that must use alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I created the namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege multi-tenant setup as requested. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support targeted NetworkPolicies (e.g., access=dev on developer namespaces, access=dev-shared on dev-shared)

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Own-namespace access:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding the user and their SA to ClusterRole admin (full namespace admin without cluster-wide privileges)
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Shared namespace read-only:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding alice, bob, charlie and their SAs to ClusterRole view (read-only; no writes, cannot view Secrets)
- Staging/prod:
  - No developer bindings. Only cluster-admins can access by default (principle of least privilege).

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared: requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod: requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) NetworkPolicies (CNI must support NetworkPolicy)
- Default deny (Ingress+Egress) in all six namespaces (not applied to system namespaces).
- DNS egress allowed from all six namespaces to CoreDNS in kube-system (UDP/TCP 53), matching common labels (k8s-app=coredns or kube-dns).
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow same-namespace ingress and egress (intra-namespace only).
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only (namespaceSelector access=dev-shared).
  - No cross-developer communication permitted.
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from developer namespaces only (namespaceSelector access=dev).
  - Allow same-namespace ingress/egress.
- staging and prod:
  - Default deny, plus allow same-namespace ingress/egress and DNS egress only.
  - No traffic to/from any dev namespaces (isolated).

Notes and validation
- I briefly created a very broad ClusterRole but removed it to adhere to least privilege. We’re using the built-in admin ClusterRole for per-namespace full control and view for read-only.
- If pods need to access additional “system services” beyond DNS (e.g., the Kubernetes API via kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add a targeted egress exception (typically via ipBlock or a controlled egress policy) per your requirements.
- Validate RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-bob --as alice     -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice        -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n dev-shared --as alice     -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice           -> no
- Validate NetworkPolicy (example quick checks):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a service in dev-shared -> allowed
  - From a pod in dev-alice, connect to a service in dev-bob    -> denied
  - From a pod in staging/prod, connect to dev namespaces       -> denied
  - DNS lookups (UDP/TCP 53 to CoreDNS) work in all six namespaces

Optional next steps (on request)
- Add LimitRanges to set default requests/limits per namespace to make quotas predictable.
- Add Pod Security Admission labels (baseline/restricted) to reduce pod privilege in dev/staging/prod.
- Issue SA tokens or short-lived projected tokens for CI/CD that must use alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa.

Done.

What I created
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) for stable network IDs
- StatefulSet: db with 3 replicas
  - Container: busybox sleeping
  - initContainer writes initial_data to /data/test if it doesn’t exist
  - volumeClaimTemplates: 1Gi PVC per pod mounted at /data
  - PVC retention on scale/delete is set to Retain so data persists
- Scaled StatefulSet db down to 1 replica

How to verify
- Pods and scale:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get sts db
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -o wide
- PVCs:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get pvc
- Data on surviving pod:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-0 -- sh -c 'ls -l /data && cat /data/test'
- (Optional) Re-scale to 3 and verify data persisted:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test scale sts/db --replicas=3
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-1 -- cat /data/test
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-2 -- cat /data/test

Notes
- If your cluster has no default StorageClass, the PVCs will remain Pending and pods won’t start. Configure a default StorageClass or specify one in the StatefulSet if needed.
